Markov chain approximating a continuous transition kernel by quadrature

Source: R/quadrature.R
fitFunction.Rd

Builds a finite-state Markov chain from a transition density (or any non-negative transition kernel) of a continuous-state process, by evaluating the kernel at the nodes of a quadrature rule (the Nystrom method). It is the counterpart of PyDTMC's fit_function.

Usage

fitFunction(
  f,
  size,
  quadrature = c("gauss-legendre", "gauss-chebyshev", "fejer", "gauss-hermite",
    "trapezoid", "simpson", "midpoint"),
  interval = c(0, 1),
  mean = 0,
  sd = 1,
  states = NULL,
  name = NULL
)

Arguments

f

A function of two arguments, f(x, y), returning the (unnormalized) density of moving from x to y. It should be vectorized: it is called once with two vectors of length size^2. A function that is not vectorized also works (it is then called once per pair), more slowly. Values must be finite and non-negative.

size

A single integer of at least 2: the number of nodes, i.e. of states of the chain.

quadrature

The quadrature rule, one of "gauss-legendre" (the default), "gauss-chebyshev", "fejer", "gauss-hermite", "trapezoid", "simpson" and "midpoint"; see Details.

interval

A numeric vector c(a, b) with a < b, the interval on which the process lives, for every rule except "gauss-hermite".

mean, sd

Mean and standard deviation of the normal distribution that defines the nodes of "gauss-hermite", which covers the whole real line; ignored by the other rules.

states

Optional character vector of size distinct state names. By default the nodes, formatted to 4 significant digits, are used (or "1", ..., "size" if that formatting is not unique).

name

Optional name of the chain.

Value

A list with three elements:

chain

The markovchain object (row-stochastic).

states

The nodes, a numeric vector named by the states, in the order of the states of chain.

weights

The quadrature weights for the plain integral \(\int g(y)\,dy \approx \sum_j w_j g(y_j)\), named by the states.

Details

With nodes \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\) and weights \(w_1, \ldots, w_n\) of a rule for \(\int g(y)\,dy\), the transition matrix is $$P_{ij} = \frac{w_j f(y_i, y_j)}{\sum_{k} w_k f(y_i, y_k)}.$$ If \(f(x, \cdot)\) is the transition density of the continuous process, \(\sum_j P_{ij} h(y_j)\) approximates \(E[h(Y_{t+1}) \mid Y_t = y_i]\) for every smooth \(h\), and the normalization corrects the mass lost outside the nodes. The kernel does not need to integrate to one: only its values at the nodes matter.

The rules, all with positive weights:

  • "gauss-legendre": Gauss-Legendre nodes, exact for polynomials of degree \(2n - 1\). A good default for smooth kernels on a bounded interval.

  • "gauss-chebyshev": Gauss-Chebyshev nodes of the first kind, \(t_k = -\cos((2k - 1)\pi / (2n))\) on \([-1, 1]\), with the weights \((\pi/n)\sqrt{1 - t_k^2}\) of a plain integral. It is exact for \(g(t) = q(t)/\sqrt{1 - t^2}\) with \(q\) a polynomial of degree \(2n - 1\), so it suits kernels with that kind of behaviour at the end points.

  • "fejer": Fejer's first rule, the same Chebyshev nodes with the weights that integrate exactly every polynomial of degree \(n - 1\). This is the rule that PyDTMC calls "gauss-chebyshev".

  • "gauss-hermite": Gauss-Hermite nodes for the normal distribution \(N(\code{mean}, \code{sd}^2)\), for processes on the real line. The weights of the plain integral are the probability weights divided by the normal density at the nodes. With an AR(1) density this is the method of Tauchen and Hussey (1991); see tauchenHussey.

  • "trapezoid" and "simpson": equally spaced nodes including the end points; Simpson's rule needs an odd size.

  • "midpoint": the centres of size equal cells.

Newton-Cotes rules of high order are not offered, because their weights become negative and would give negative probabilities.

A row whose kernel values are all zero at the nodes (the process cannot reach any node from there) stops the function with an error: PyDTMC replaces such a row with a uniform distribution, which invents transitions; here the interval, the number of nodes or the kernel should be changed instead.

For the same kernel, interval and number of nodes, the "gauss-legendre", "fejer", "trapezoid" and "simpson" rules give the same matrices as PyDTMC 10.0.0 ("gauss-legendre", "gauss-chebyshev", "trapezoid-rule" and "simpson-rule"); PyDTMC's midpoint rule ("newton-cotes") ignores the lower end of the interval.

References

Tauchen, G. and Hussey, R. (1991). Quadrature-based methods for obtaining approximate solutions to nonlinear asset pricing models. Econometrica, 59(2), 371-396. doi:10.2307/2938261

Golub, G. H. and Welsch, J. H. (1969). Calculation of Gauss quadrature rules. Mathematics of Computation, 23(106), 221-230. doi:10.2307/2004418

Fejer, L. (1933). Mechanische Quadraturen mit positiven Cotesschen Zahlen. Mathematische Zeitschrift, 37, 287-309. doi:10.1007/BF01474575

See also

tauchenHussey, tauchen, rouwenhorst

Examples

# A process on [0, 1] that moves towards 0.6 times its current value,
# with a Gaussian kernel truncated to the interval.
kernel <- function(x, y) dnorm(y, mean = 0.6 * x + 0.2, sd = 0.15)
out <- fitFunction(kernel, size = 7, interval = c(0, 1))
out$chain
#> Quadrature approximation (gauss-legendre, 7 nodes) 
#>  A  7 - dimensional discrete Markov Chain defined by the following states: 
#>  0.02545, 0.12920, 0.29710, 0.50000, 0.70290, 0.87080, 0.97460 
#>  The transition matrix  (by rows)  is defined as follows: 
#>              0.02545      0.12920     0.29710   0.50000     0.70290
#> 0.02545 8.360400e-02 3.412097e-01 0.473186072 0.0991878 0.002783226
#> 0.12920 4.333595e-02 2.357194e-01 0.520178020 0.1912008 0.009407870
#> 0.29710 1.090360e-02 9.437633e-02 0.441444909 0.4024013 0.049102801
#> 0.50000 1.155157e-03 1.753256e-02 0.203378028 0.5558685 0.203378028
#> 0.70290 6.413373e-05 1.706878e-03 0.049102801 0.4024013 0.441444909
#> 0.87080 3.643080e-06 1.542875e-04 0.009407870 0.1912008 0.520178020
#> 0.97460 5.081911e-07 2.868414e-05 0.002783226 0.0991878 0.473186072
#>              0.87080      0.97460
#> 0.02545 2.868414e-05 5.081911e-07
#> 0.12920 1.542875e-04 3.643080e-06
#> 0.29710 1.706878e-03 6.413373e-05
#> 0.50000 1.753256e-02 1.155157e-03
#> 0.70290 9.437633e-02 1.090360e-02
#> 0.87080 2.357194e-01 4.333595e-02
#> 0.97460 3.412097e-01 8.360400e-02
#> 
# expected next value from each node, against the continuous one
cbind(chain = as.numeric(out$chain@transitionMatrix %*% out$states),
      target = 0.6 * out$states + 0.2)
#>             chain    target
#> 0.02545 0.2383721 0.2152676
